32.stem: A strain is BEST defined as an injury to a:
choices: Ligament connecting bone to bone
Muscle or tendon
Articular cartilage only
Bone shaft with displacement from the joint
32.why: Strain = muscle/tendon. Sprain = ligament. Dislocation = bone out of joint.

32.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a strain from a sprain?
choices: A strain involves ligaments; a sprain involves muscle
A strain involves muscle or tendon; a sprain involves ligaments
Both terms mean the same injury to a joint capsule
A sprain always includes a complete bone fracture
32.why: Remember: sTrain → Tendon/muscle; sPrain → ligament (joint).

32.stem: Field care for an open fracture includes all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Control bleeding and cover the wound with a sterile dressing
Splint the extremity and check distal CSM
Push bone ends back under the skin to close the wound
Treat for shock and transport
32.why: Never force bone ends back under the skin. Cover, control bleeding, splint, transport.

32.stem: You find bone protruding through the skin of a forearm. After scene safety and ABCs, your NEXT priority is to:
choices: Irrigate the wound with hydrogen peroxide until clean
Control hemorrhage and cover the open wound with a sterile dressing before splinting
Attempt closed reduction in the field
Apply a traction splint to the forearm
32.why: Open fracture = soft-tissue wound plus broken bone. Stop bleeding, sterile cover, then immobilize.

32.stem: A sling and swathe is MOST appropriate to immobilize a:
choices: Isolated mid-shaft femur fracture
Suspected clavicle or shoulder injury
Unstable pelvic ring fracture
Open tibial fracture with arterial bleeding only
32.why: Sling supports the arm; swathe binds it to the chest — classic for clavicle/shoulder girdle injuries.

32.stem: The purpose of the swathe when using a sling and swathe is to:
choices: Apply circumferential traction to the humerus
Hold the arm against the chest to limit shoulder motion
Replace the need for a distal CSM check
Reduce a dislocated hip at the scene
32.why: The swathe secures the arm to the torso so the shoulder cannot swing freely.

32.stem: When splinting a suspected joint injury (for example, an elbow), you should generally:
choices: Force the joint through full range of motion first
Immobilize the joint and the bones above and below it in the position found
Apply a traction splint across the joint
Leave the joint free so the patient can "work out" the injury
32.why: Joint injuries: splint as found, immobilizing the joint plus adjacent long bones.

32.stem: Proper immobilization of a long-bone fracture requires that the splint:
choices: Immobilize only the fracture site itself
Immobilize the joints above and below the fracture
Always include a traction device regardless of location
Be applied before any wound care on an open fracture
32.why: Long bone rule: joints above and below. Joint rule: bones above and below.

32.stem: An angulated closed forearm fracture has no distal pulse. Per common EMT training, you should:
choices: Leave it severely angulated and never attempt realignment
Gently attempt realignment once toward anatomic position, then splint and recheck CSM
Forcefully crank the limb until it "pops" into place repeatedly
Apply a traction splint designed for the femur
32.why: No distal pulse after position-found care → gentle realignment once (if trained/protocol), then splint and reassess.

32.stem: If gentle realignment of an angulated fracture restores a distal pulse, you should NEXT:
choices: Immediately reverse the realignment to the original angle
Splint in the improved position and recheck CSM frequently
Have the patient walk to stretch the vessels
Remove all dressings so the skin can "breathe"
32.why: Keep the improved alignment with a good splint and keep checking neurovascular status.

32.stem: Field management of a suspected shoulder dislocation typically includes:
choices: Forceful field reduction by yanking the arm overhead
Supporting the arm in the position of comfort (often sling/swathe) and transporting
Applying a femoral traction splint to the upper extremity
Having the patient do push-ups to relocate the humeral head
32.why: EMTs do not force shoulder reductions. Support as found/comfort, protect, transport.

32.stem: A patient holds the injured arm away from the body and reports sudden shoulder pain after a fall. You note a squared-off shoulder contour. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
choices: An isolated mid-shaft femur fracture
A shoulder dislocation
A greenstick fracture of the tibia
Compartment syndrome of the calf
32.why: Squared shoulder, arm held slightly abducted/supported = classic anterior shoulder dislocation picture.

32.stem: A patient who fell onto the shoulder reports pain over the mid-clavicle and supports the arm against the chest. Appropriate EMT care is to:
choices: Apply a traction splint to the clavicle
Immobilize with a sling and swathe and check distal CSM
Force the clavicle ends into alignment with manual pressure
Ignore the injury because clavicle fractures never bleed
32.why: Clavicle: sling/swathe, CSM, ice if protocol, transport. Do not "set" it in the field.

32.stem: Clavicle fractures are commonly associated with which mechanism?
choices: Direct blow or fall onto the shoulder; sometimes FOOSH transmitted force
Isolated twisting of the ankle only
Crush injury confined to the toes
Hyperflexion of the lumbar spine alone
32.why: Fall on shoulder or FOOSH force up the arm can fracture the clavicle — common in bikes/scooters.

32.stem: A teen falls from a scooter and braces with an outstretched hand (FOOSH). Which injury pattern should you specifically assess for?
choices: Wrist, forearm, elbow, or clavicle/shoulder girdle injury
Isolated calcaneus fracture only
Pelvic binder indication without any trunk MOI
Guaranteed mid-shaft femur fracture requiring traction
32.why: FOOSH transmits force up the kinetic chain — wrist/forearm, elbow, and sometimes clavicle/shoulder.

32.stem: Care of a completely amputated part includes wrapping it in dry sterile dressings, placing it in a plastic bag, and then:
choices: Packing it directly in dry ice so it freezes solid
Keeping it cool by placing the bag on ice (not in direct contact with ice/water)
Soaking it in warm sterile saline for the entire transport
Discarding it if transport time exceeds 10 minutes
32.why: Dry sterile wrap → bag → cool with ice (part stays dry; no direct ice contact). Transport with the patient.

32.stem: Which action is INCORRECT when managing an amputated body part?
choices: Control bleeding on the stump with direct pressure and a pressure dressing
Keep the amputated part with the patient during transport
Immerse the amputated part directly in ice water
Label the bag with the patient's name and time of injury when possible
32.why: Never put the part directly in ice or water — frostbite/tissue damage ruins reimplantation chances.

32.stem: Compared with a sprain, a fracture is MORE likely to present with:
choices: Only mild joint stiffness without tenderness
Deformity, crepitus, and point tenderness over a bone
Completely normal use of the limb in all cases
Pain limited exclusively to muscle belly stretch
32.why: Fracture clues: deformity, crepitus, bony point tenderness. Sprains are ligamentous around a joint.

32.stem: A dislocation differs from a fracture primarily because a dislocation involves:
choices: A break in the continuity of bone only
Displacement of a bone end from its normal position in a joint
Injury limited to muscle fibers remote from any joint
Always an open wound over the injury site
32.why: Dislocation = bone out of joint. Fracture = break in bone. Both can coexist (fracture-dislocation).

32.stem: A patient twisted an ankle. The joint is swollen and tender but has no gross deformity and can still move somewhat. This is MOST consistent with a:
choices: Complete mid-shaft femur fracture
Sprain
Open skull fracture
Pathologic hip dislocation requiring field reduction
32.why: Sprains: joint pain/swelling without the dramatic deformity of many dislocations/fractures — still splint and transport if unsure.

32.stem: A greenstick fracture is BEST described as:
choices: A complete break through both cortices with free bone ends in an adult femur
An incomplete fracture in which the bone bends and cracks on one side, common in children
A fracture that occurs only through metastatic cancer deposits
Displacement of the femoral head from the acetabulum
32.why: Kids' bones are flexible — greenstick = incomplete bend/break, like a green twig.

32.stem: A pathologic fracture is one that:
choices: Occurs only during high-speed motor vehicle crashes
Occurs through bone weakened by disease (e.g., cancer, osteoporosis) often with minimal force
Always involves an open wound and protruding bone
Is defined solely by the presence of a joint dislocation
32.why: Pathologic = diseased/weak bone fails under little or no trauma. Treat the fracture and the patient.

32.stem: An elderly woman with known osteoporosis falls on an outstretched hand. Which injury is especially common in this population?
choices: Distal radius (wrist) fracture
Isolated midfoot sprain that never needs evaluation
Guaranteed bilateral femur fractures requiring dual traction
Greenstick fractures of both tibias only
32.why: Osteoporotic FOOSH → distal radius (Colles-type) is classic in older adults; also think hip/humerus.

32.stem: After an elderly FOOSH injury, EMS should also carefully assess for:
choices: Associated head injury, other fractures, and ability to ambulate safely
Only the wrist, because FOOSH never affects anything else
Immediate need for a pelvic binder without examining the pelvis
Mandatory field reduction of every wrist deformity
32.why: Falls in the elderly are multi-injury events — wrist plus head, hip, spine, and functional status.

32.stem: A patient has an isolated injury involving the knee joint with deformity. You should:
choices: Apply a standard femoral traction splint across the knee
Splint the knee in the position found and avoid traction-splint application
Force the knee into full extension before any immobilization
Walk the patient to stretch the joint capsule
32.why: Knee (and hip/ankle) injuries contraindicate traction splints. Splint as found; protect distal CSM.

32.stem: Which statement about knee injuries is MOST accurate for EMT care?
choices: All knee injuries should receive a traction splint
Immobilize as found; pad voids; check distal CSM; do not use femoral traction
Always reduce patellar dislocations with vigorous traction
Knee injuries never threaten neurovascular status
32.why: Position found, good padding, CSM checks. Traction splints are for mid-shaft femur — not the knee.

32.stem: A common method to immobilize an injured ankle when using a soft or pillow splint is a:
choices: Stirrup-style wrap that supports the foot and ankle
Femoral traction hitch applied at the toes
Pelvic binder cinched around the malleoli
Sling and swathe of the lower leg to the chest
32.why: Stirrup (U-shaped) support cradles heel/ankle; then secure and check CSM.

32.stem: When splinting a suspected ankle fracture, you should:
choices: Remove the shoe only if it interferes with assessment/care, then immobilize foot-ankle-lower leg
Always force the ankle into a 90° angle regardless of pain or pulses
Apply a traction splint as first-line care
Leave the injury unsupported so swelling can "drain"
32.why: Expose as needed for CSM/wound care, then immobilize the foot, ankle, and distal tibia/fibula region.

32.stem: A rigid splint is MOST useful when you need to:
choices: Conform loosely around a massively swollen joint without structure
Provide firm immobilization of a straight long-bone segment
Replace hemorrhage control on a spurting artery
Apply continuous mechanical traction to the pelvis
32.why: Rigid (board/SAM-type) splints give firm support for relatively straight limb segments.

32.stem: A soft (pillow or blanket) splint is often preferred for:
choices: Isolated mid-shaft femur fractures requiring traction
Ankle or foot injuries where conforming support reduces pain
Unstable pelvic fractures as the sole definitive hospital care
Replacing sterile dressings on open fractures
32.why: Soft/pillow splints mold to irregular shapes — great for ankles/feet when secured well.

32.stem: In musculoskeletal assessment, CSM and PMS refer to the same distal neurovascular check. CSM stands for:
choices: Circulation, Sensory, Motor
Compression, Splint, Mobility
Crepitus, Swelling, Mobility
Color, Shock, Mentation
32.why: CSM = Circulation, Sensory, Motor. PMS = Pulse, Motor, Sensation. Same idea, different letters.

32.stem: When instructors say "check CSM," they want you to evaluate distal:
choices: Only capillary refill, ignoring movement and feeling
Pulse/circulation, sensation, and motor function
Only the patient's ability to walk
Only skin temperature proximal to the injury
32.why: Distal pulse/perfusion, can they feel, can they move — before and after every splint.

32.stem: The "six Ps" associated with compartment syndrome and limb ischemia include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Pain and Pressure (or Pallor)
Paresthesia and Paralysis
Pulselessness and Poikilothermia (coolness)
Polydipsia and Polyuria
32.why: Six Ps: Pain, Pallor, Paresthesia, Pulselessness, Paralysis, Poikilothermia (Pressure). Polydipsia/polyuria = diabetes.

32.stem: Which finding is a LATE sign of compartment syndrome?
choices: Pain with passive stretch of the affected muscles
Increasing pain and tense swelling of the compartment
Absence of a distal pulse
Patient anxiety about the injury
32.why: Pulselessness comes late. Early: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch.

32.stem: A high-energy trauma patient has pelvic instability and signs of shock. Your priorities include:
choices: Minimizing pelvic motion, considering a binder per protocol, and rapid transport while treating shock
Walking the patient to "settle" the pelvis
Applying bilateral femoral traction splints as primary pelvic care
Delaying transport until the pelvis is surgically fixed on scene
32.why: Pelvic fractures can hide massive hemorrhage. Limit movement, binder if trained, shock care, go.

32.stem: Blood loss from an unstable pelvic fracture is dangerous mainly because:
choices: It is always limited to less than 100 mL
Retroperitoneal and pelvic bleeding can be massive without much external blood
It only causes problems if the skin is open
It never produces hypotension
32.why: Pelvis can hold liters of blood. Shock may precede dramatic external bleeding.

32.stem: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is BEST understood by EMTs as:
choices: A pediatric/adolescent hip problem where the femoral head slips at the growth plate — do not force the hip
An adult-only mid-shaft femur fracture treated with traction every time
A type of greenstick fracture of the clavicle
A wrist sprain from FOOSH that never needs evaluation
32.why: SCFE: kid/teen hip/thigh/knee pain, often after growth spurt — immobilize gently, no forced ROM, transport.

32.stem: An overweight 12-year-old has groin and knee pain and limps after minor activity. Suspect a hip growth-plate problem and:
choices: Encourage running to "loosen" the joint
Minimize weight-bearing, support the limb, and transport for evaluation
Apply a traction splint across the pelvis
Perform forceful field reduction of the femoral head
32.why: Possible SCFE/hip pathology — off the leg, gentle care, hospital evaluation. No field hip tricks.

32.stem: Crepitus on exam of an injured limb MOST strongly suggests:
choices: A simple muscle strain without bone involvement
Fractured bone ends grating against each other
A sprain limited to ligament stretch only
Normal joint lubrication
32.why: Crepitus = grating of fracture fragments. Stop grinding it — splint and reassess CSM.

32.stem: The general rule for musculoskeletal immobilization is to:
choices: Splint before exposing life-threatening hemorrhage
Expose the injury, control bleeding, dress open wounds, then splint while protecting distal CSM
Always straighten every deformity before ABCs
Never check distal neurovascular status after the splint is on
32.why: Life threats first, then wound care, then splint — with distal checks built into the skill.
